description: Correspondence studies send matched CVs differing only in name and measure callback rates. The design is well established across many labour markets.
notes: The METHOD is well established; I have not verified an Iranian-specific study here. Layer-5 target: locate audit studies covering Iranian or Persian names specifically, rather than generalising from Arab/Muslim-name studies, which is a different population.

description: Many people adopt a shortened or Anglicised name on the CV. Where it works, it is evidence the discrimination was real; the cost is carried privately.
energy_note: Editing your own name to be employable.

description: An applicant delayed two years by security screening also carries an unexplained employment gap, which is independently penalised.

Omid's CV has a 26-month gap where a security screening ran. Every interviewer asks about it. 'I was waiting for a government decision' sounds, to a hiring manager who has never waited for one, like an evasion.
energy_note: Penalised twice: once for the delay, once for having to describe it.

description: Worldwide experimental data show minority-signalling candidates receive on average 29% fewer positive responses, with penalties as high as 41% for Arab applicants and as low as 8% for Hispanic applicants. Middle Easterners consistently rank among the most penalised groups.
energy_note: Not a feeling. A measured coefficient.
notes: ANSWERS EMP-003-001, partly. See the row below for the Iranian-specific gap.

aspect: NO study isolates Persian or Iranian names
description: Audit studies fold Iranians into a broad 'Middle Eastern' or 'Arab/Muslim' treatment. There is no dedicated experiment separating Persian names - a real limitation, given Iranians are not Arab.
energy_note: Measured as a category you are not a member of.
notes: ANSWERS EMP-003-001. This is also the empirical version of PSY-009: the conflation is not only cultural, it is baked into the research.

description: Candidates with Swedish names received 50% more callbacks than those with Middle Eastern names.

A large audit using Anglo-Saxon, Indigenous, Italian, Chinese and Middle Eastern names on otherwise identical entry-level CVs - all showing Australian schooling - found economically and statistically significant callback differences, with Italians facing less discrimination than Chinese and Middle Easterners.

Using a Bertrand-Mullainathan design, résumés with Arabic names received fewer callbacks than white-sounding names. Derous et al. (2009) found moderate discrimination against Arabic names in a résumé-sorting task.

Applicants are less likely to be called back when their names are difficult to pronounce - a finding that holds within immigrant groups, so it operates independently of ethnic animus. Persian names vary widely in distinctiveness and pronounceability, from Reza to Darius.
energy_note: Penalised for the number of syllables.
source_name: Hamilton College working paper on name pronunciation

aspect: Callback gaps understate the real gap
description: Quillian et al. (2020) document larger majority-minority differences at the job-offer stage than at callback - so audit studies, which measure only the first screen, are conservative estimates.

Darolia et al. (2016) found no callback discrimination across 9,000 résumés when pairing typically-white first names with typically-black last names - though critics argue the name signals may have been misread nearly 60% of the time. The debate about signal strength applies directly to Persian names.
notes: Included for balance. The effect is well established; the magnitude is genuinely contested.
